tagline: From seaside cliffs to inland valleys, a coast road joined by bridges.
intro: Oregon’s Pacific Coast Scenic Byway follows US 101 between seaside cliffs, marshes, agricultural valleys and dunes, moving inland and back to the sea. It is an All-American Road, whose coastal scenery, historic bridges and lighthouses feature in the Federal Highway Administration’s description. Oregon’s transportation department recommends a minimum of ten to twelve hours of driving and several days for the trip. For most of its Oregon length, US 101 is an undivided two-lane highway, frequently mountainous between the ocean and Coast Range.

Before the automobile highway, coastal travel depended on boats and beach routes. Approved in 1919 as the Roosevelt Coast Military Highway, the road entered construction in 1921 and became part of US 101 in 1926. Six ferry crossings interrupted the highway; even extended state-run schedules failed to keep up with motorists. Five bridges designed by state engineer Conde B. McCullough replaced ferries between 1934 and 1936, and the highway was declared complete that October.

Start in Astoria and travel south through Seaside to Cannon Beach and Haystack Rock. The road turns inland toward Tillamook, then returns to the coast north of Lincoln City. Continue through Newport and Yachats to Cape Perpetua, then Florence and the dunes. Farther south come Coos Bay, Bandon, Gold Beach at the Rogue River’s mouth, and Brookings.
notice: In Newport, Yaquina Bay Lighthouse combines its light and living quarters in one building.

moments.title: Haystack Rock
moments.text: At Cannon Beach, a 235-foot basalt sea stack rises beside the beach. Haystack Rock was once connected to the coast; erosion separated it from the mainland. At low tide, a strip of rock and sand connects the beach to the stack, with tide pools holding sea anemones, crabs, limpets and sea slugs. The rock also provides nesting sites for seabirds, including puffins. Three smaller formations to the south are called the Needles. Oregon granted Haystack Rock Marine Garden status in 1990; the stack also lies within the Oregon Islands National Wildlife Refuge’s designated wilderness.
moments.notice: The three smaller rock formations south of Haystack Rock are the Needles.

moments.title: Cape Perpetua
moments.text: A road cut into Cape Perpetua’s cliff opened travel between Yachats and Florence in 1914. The Forest Service paired that narrow road with a wooden bridge across the Yachats River; the bridge was replaced with steel in 1926. The highway section followed in the 1930s. This forested headland rises above 800 feet. On a clear day, the crest offers a view along 70 miles of Oregon coastline. The Civilian Conservation Corps built trails and the West Shelter observation point near the top; during World War II, that shelter served as a coastal watch station.

moments.title: Oregon Dunes
moments.text: South of Florence, the coastal landscape opens into dunes, some reaching 500 feet above sea level. The national recreation area stretches approximately 40 miles between Florence and North Bend. Oregon’s transportation department describes sand derived from eroded mountain rock, carried to the ocean and washed inland by tides. The moving sand also entered literature: Frank Herbert’s research and fascination with this area helped inspire his science-fiction novel Dune. A national recreation area was established in 1972, protecting 32,186 acres under legislation sponsored by Congressman John R. Dellenback; it remains administered by the Forest Service.
